What happened

Switching on the new progress-tracking feature broke a different page

Right after we turned the feature on, our own automated checks hit this error on any campaign page with a completed participant — the screen on the left is that actual error. Security and scale, checked against the code

Beyond the features themselves, we ran a deliberate check against the pitfalls that quietly break apps at scale: leaked credentials, broken access control, missing rate limits, unhandled errors, and inefficient database queries. Three fixes shipped as real pull requests on June 22–24, each with before/after tests. Here's the honest per-item result — including the two that are only partly done.

Credentials
Data access
Rate limits
Error handling
DB queries
Authorization
Not present

No credentials have ever been committed

Only a template env file with placeholder values is tracked in the repository; the real environment files are excluded everywhere. We also scanned every historical change ever made to an env file, across all branches, for patterns that look like live keys — none found.

That scan is a targeted check, not a full secret-scanner run. Worth doing once for full certainty rather than "nothing noticed."
Different model, same protection

Access control lives in application code, not database policies

The database doesn't use row-level security policies — it's plain Postgres, with per-org and per-file access checked in code before any query runs. That's a different mechanism than some setups use, not a gap by itself. The real version of this risk — "can one user see another user's data" — is what the authorization fix below actually addresses.

Partially true — being straight about it

Some critical routes are rate-limited. Most of the codebase still isn't.

File uploads and invite-acceptance were specifically hardened. Counting it directly across every API route in the app: 46 of 129 call the rate-limit check today.

46 / 129 routes rate-limited
The other ~83 routes are not individually confirmed. Not calling this one done.
Found and fixed where checked

An unhandled-error bug was real — three instances, all fixed

79ff86e — error-handling hardeningsurveys/[id]/submit/route.ts
- const bodyValidation = schema.safeParse(await request.json());+ let rawBody: unknown;+ try { rawBody = await request.json(); }+ catch { return NextResponse.json({ error: "Invalid JSON body" }, { status: 400 }); }+ const bodyValidation = schema.safeParse(rawBody);

Before this, a malformed request on the public survey-submit endpoint threw an unhandled 500 straight from the JSON parse. The same fix also stopped a one-time failed email-server check from permanently blocking retries, and wrapped a scheduling route's database and job-queue calls so an outage returns a clean error instead of crashing.

Scoped as three specific instances that were found and fixed — not a claim that every possible failure path in the codebase is now caught.
Found and fixed on the write path — read path deferred, on record

A real inefficient-query pattern was found inside a database lock

6b2cd4f — batch insertsassessment-campaigns/[id]/participants/route.ts
// before: up to 500 sequential inserts in a loop- for (const r of respondentsToAdd) {-   await tx.assessmentCampaignParticipant.create({ data: {...} });- }// after: one batched insert+ await tx.assessmentCampaignParticipant.createMany({ data: createData });

A sharper fix in the same pass: a workload check was running one query per affected coach while holding a database lock — fine at small scale, a real contention risk under load. Collapsed into a single grouped query.

This covered the write-heavy paths that were flagged. A handful of read-side inefficiencies (a bulk-import check, two page load consolidations, list pagination) were identified and deliberately deferred, on record in the project plan — not silently skipped.
A real one — found and closed

Any logged-in coach could read another coach's file link

17af202 — close broken authorizationfiles/[id]/route.ts
  export async function GET(...) {-   if (!session?.user) return unauthorized();+   if (!actor) return unauthorized();    ...+   // Reading metadata exposes the direct file link — gate it+   // with the same read policy as the download route.+   if (!canReadFile({ actor, file })) return forbidden();

Before this fix, the check was only "is someone logged in" — not "does this person own this file." Any authenticated coach could fetch another coach's file metadata, including its direct download link. The same fix closed a second case where a coach could create or duplicate workflows through a direct API call even though the button was hidden in their view — a backend check standing in for a frontend-only restriction.

109 / 129 API routes resolve an authenticated identity before acting; the remainder match documented public routes (webhooks, public registration, auth flows).

Being straight about status

Live and verified — not yet confirmed with real coaches

Everything shown above shipped to production during this window — much of it went live on June 30, when a batch of previously-dark features was switched on. We verified each one ourselves. As of this update we don't yet have confirmation that real coaches have started using the newest pieces day to day — that's the next thing we'll watch for.

The full roadmap, zoomed out

"Bringing your history over" is one piece of a bigger plan. Today we went through every screen in the assessment admin and coach tools and turned what we found into a 5-phase roadmap — sequenced so we fix what's live before we protect the data, before we finish what's half-built, before we add anything new. Real screens below, not just descriptions.

Why this order: the tempting move is to build the flashier "coming soon" screens first — they demo better. We're deliberately not doing that. Stacking new features on top of unguarded data is how the next production bug gets born. Fix → protect → finish → build → polish.

Fix what shipped

Small, live bugs

Found during today's sweep — low-impact, but real.

  • A setup step for adding a branded slide before a specific section silently fails for every assessment template, because of a mismatched setting name under the hood. Nothing breaks or loses data — the slide option just doesn't show up where it should.
  • Coach identity is being matched two different ways internally (by email in one place, by account ID in another). They agree for every coach today, but they shouldn't be allowed to quietly drift apart.
1

Protect the data

Before anything new

The foundation — this is what makes every later phase safe to build on.

  • Safer version history. Old template versions get archived, never deleted outright, and a real "undo a publish" exists with a clear warning about what it affects.
  • Saves that can't half-fail. A save either fully completes or doesn't happen at all — never partially, in a way that could quietly corrupt a template.

Stop the confusion

Real screen below — this one isn't hypothetical.

  • Which version is actually live? Right now there's no way to tell — see the screen below.
  • Replace engineering terms in the admin tools with plain language throughout.
  • A clearer explanation for why a published template can't be edited directly (today it just looks broken).
The actual screen today. Look at the "Active Version Published" column — every single row shows a dash. There's no way for an admin to tell which version of a template is the one actually live for new campaigns. That's what Phase 2 fixes: a clear "LIVE" badge on the version that's really in use.

Studied the real historical files

Three independent review passes, each hunting for a different kind of problem: security holes, mixed-up company data, and operational risk. 26 issues turned up across the three rounds — every one fixed in the plan before any code was written.

Built the safe plumbingJust shipped · July 1

The part that accepts a coach's uploaded historical files — with every safety check in place: duplicate-round detection, wrong-company protection, incomplete-data checks, and a check that the coach explicitly picks which company the data belongs to (never guessed from the file).

The screen that just shipped. The new "SU-Full (historical)" option, with the round label, the explicit "Target organization" (note: "Chosen explicitly — never guessed from the file contents"), and the multi-file upload. How this was captured, honestly: this screen is switched off in production, so it can't be photographed there. This is the real, just-merged code running in a developer test environment with the switch manually forced on — proof the screen is built, not a mockup. A coach can't see this yet.

Why it's not switched on yet — the real reason

The piece that translates each old Esperto question into its new equivalent doesn't exist yet. What shipped is all the plumbing around it — the upload, the safety checks, the storage. The actual question-by-question mapping is deliberately still an empty placeholder.

So if we turned the feature on today, it would cleanly refuse every import rather than guess. That's on purpose. Guessing that mapping wrong would silently file someone's old answers under the wrong questions and quietly corrupt their history — and that's the one mistake here that's genuinely hard to undo.

It stays off until, in order: (1) that mapping is written, (2) a person checks it line-by-line against the original Esperto reports and signs off, and only then (3) it's switched on gradually — our pilot account first, then a few coaches, then everyone. Best estimate for that verification work: about a week. We have the source material to do it — it's not waiting on anyone else.

Three problems found and fixed mid-build — including one that would have crashed on deploy — before this went up for review.

4

Make the assessment editor less intimidating

Not started — last on purpose

To be clear: this is a future phase — nothing here is built yet. It's about one specific screen, the tool admins use to build an assessment. Here's the concrete problem it fixes:

The actual editor today. This is the real screen an admin sees when building an assessment. Notice it reads like an engineering console: tabs like "Scoring & Tiers," a greyed-out "Conditional Logic" option that doesn't work yet, and raw computer strings like the "content hash" (9a23eca13955…) in the version list. Functional, but daunting if you're not technical.

What this phase will do about it, once we get to it:

  • Let an admin start from a ready-made, filled-in template instead of a blank, intimidating form.
  • Tuck the advanced settings (scoring math, question logic) behind an "advanced" option — there for anyone who wants them, out of the way by default.
  • Replace the computer-speak with plain language and a live preview, so it reads like a normal product.

No screenshot of the "after" — it doesn't exist yet. That's the honest status: identified, planned, not built.
